name: Peronism
summary: Peronism, also called Justicialism, is the Argentine movement built around Juan and Eva Perón. It joins state-guided industrial development, strong state-sponsored unions and social rights with class harmony under a central leader, nationalism, economic independence and a Third Position between capitalism and communism, and holds property to a social function.
scope: Classical Peronism as Perón set it out and as it governed Argentina in 1946-1955: the Twenty Truths of Justicialism (1950), the 1949 constitution enacted under it, the record of those governments described in the encyclopedias, and Perón's mature restatement in the Modelo argentino (1974). Later strands (Menemist market reform, Kirchnerism, the Montoneros and other revolutionary Peronism) are other subjects and are excluded; scholarship says these held conflicting ideologies under the same name. Peronism's own record is that of the 1946-1955 governments, when it was the official doctrine of the state.

notes: Themes searched: economy and property, labour, government and elections, rights and liberty, family and religion, ecology, science and technology, foreign policy and sovereignty, the armed forces, education and culture. Answers rest on the 1949 constitution and the encyclopedias' account of the 1946-1955 record where there is a record, and on Perón's Twenty Truths and Modelo (1974) where there is none. The Modelo is a 1974 text whose drafting by Perón alone is disputed; it was edited and published after his death and is used as his doctrinal testament. Earlier answers that rested on Wikipedia were nulled or rebuilt on these sources. Not searched in depth: Perón's 1946 to 1955 speeches in Spanish, the Five-Year Plans, and Conducción política (saved in the library, not cited), so health, tax, justice and many social-issue statements stay null; the doctrine and the constitution say nothing on them. Scholars disagree on the character of Peronism (populism, fascism-affinity, an alliance of workers with the state), and the record points both ways on liberties: the constitution lists them and the governments restricted them.
